content: CYC1, also referred to as cytochrome c1, heme protein, mitochondrial (CYC1), or by other names such as UQCR4, MC3DN6, Complex III subunit 4, and cytochrome b-c1 complex subunit 4, is a protein encoded by the CYC1 gene in humans. This protein is a component of the mitochondrial respiratory chain and is specifically a subunit of ubiquinol-cytochrome c reductase (Complex III), which is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane. It plays a critical role in the electron transport chain. The CYC1 protein is composed of 130 amino acids, has a molecular weight of approximately 5 kDa, and is encoded by a gene containing 8 exons. It belongs to the cytochrome c family and functions as a phosphoprotein that binds heme groups. Structurally, it contains alpha helices, a transit peptide, and transmembrane domains, including 9 alpha helices, 5 beta strands, and 3 turns. The transmembrane region of the protein spans the inner mitochondrial membrane once, with the majority of the protein localized on the intermembrane side. CYC1 contains covalent heme-binding sites at positions 121 and 124, as well as heme axial ligand iron-metal binding sites at positions 125 and 244. Functionally, CYC1 is a respiratory subunit of the cytochrome bc1 complex, which is a key component of the mitochondrial respiratory chain. It facilitates the transfer of electrons from the Rieske iron-sulfur protein to cytochrome c, a critical step in cellular respiration and energy production. The CYC1 gene is conserved across a wide range of species, including chimpanzees, rhesus monkeys, dogs, cows, mice, rats, zebrafish, fruit flies, mosquitoes, C. elegans, S. cerevisiae, K. lactis, E. gossypii, S. pombe, N. crassa, A. thaliana, rice, and frogs. Orthologs of CYC1 have been identified in 137 known organisms. Clinically, mutations in the CYC1 gene have been associated with mitochondrial complex III deficiency, nuclear type 6. This is an autosomal recessive disorder of the mitochondrial respiratory chain caused by defects in ubiquinol-cytochrome c reductase (Complex III), leading to reduced activity of this complex. Symptoms typically manifest in early childhood and may include episodic acute lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, insulin-responsive hyperglycemia, liver dysfunction, encephalopathy, and associated infections. Despite these symptoms, psychomotor development may remain normal in some cases. A specific mutation, Leu215Phe, has been identified in association with this condition. CYC1 is known to participate in 78 protein-protein interactions, 72 of which are co-complex interactions. It is one of 11 subunits of ubiquinol-cytochrome c reductase (the bc1 complex), which includes respiratory subunits such as cytochrome b, cytochrome c1 (CYC1), UQCRFS1, core proteins UQCRC1 and UQCRC2, and low-molecular-weight proteins UQCRH, UQCRB, UQCRQ, UQCR10, and UQCR11, as well as an additional cleavage product of UQCRFS1. Furthermore, CYC1 has been found to interact with CCP1, CDKA-1, and CDKB1-1.
